# aeneid-048 — new house renderings

One set piece on the pending list falls in this part, VI.851–853, and the run decides it here (as with I.203, I.462, II.49, IV.23 and VI.126–129). It was built from the Latin and then checked against memory of the best-known modern versions for verbatim echo. Greenough's reading `pacisque` ("the custom of peace") is translated; the note gives the Latin Library's `pacique`.

| line | Latin | `l` | `i` |
|---|---|---|---|
| VI.851–853 | *tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento; / hae tibi erunt artes; pacisque imponere morem, / parcere subiectis, et debellare superbos* | "you, to rule by your command the peoples, Roman, remember; / these for you will be the arts; and of peace to impose the custom, / to spare the subjected, and to fight out the war against the proud." | "As for you, Roman, keep this in mind: your calling is to govern the peoples by your sovereign power — these will be the skills that are yours — to make peace a settled custom, to show mercy to those who submit, and to fight the arrogant to the finish." |

Echoes avoided in 851–853: the opening "But you, Roman, remember" / "Roman, remember by your strength to rule"; "with thy sway"; "these will be your arts" in `i` (kept only in `l`, where it is the bare literal of *hae tibi erunt artes*); "the habit of peace", "the ways/works of peace", "the rule of law", "crown peace with law"; "spare the conquered / defeated / vanquished / humbled"; "battle down / beat down / break / crush / tame the proud"; "war down the proud" (the literal of *debellare* in `l` was turned to "fight out the war against" for that reason). VI.847 *excudent alii* is not proposed as a house rendering: it is the lead-in, not the set piece.

For the reviewer (not proposed as house renderings), the other best-known lines of the part, built from the Latin alone:

- VI.847–850 *Excudent alii spirantia mollius aera… et surgentia sidera dicent:*
  - `l`: "Others will hammer out breathing bronzes more softly, / I believe indeed, will draw living faces out of marble, / will plead causes better, and of the heaven the motions / will mark out with the rod, and the rising stars will tell:"
  - `i`: "Others, I am sure of it, will beat out bronze that seems to breathe with a gentler skill, and coax features alive from the marble; others will argue cases more ably, map the wanderings of the sky with the pointer, and name the stars as they climb:"
  - Avoided "breathing bronze/brass", "inform the breathing brass", "I can well believe", "lifelike", "suppler lines", "plead their causes better" (in `i`), "the rising stars" (in `i`). `l` keeps the literal "breathing bronzes", "plead causes", which any word-for-word version shares.
- VI.878–879 *Heu pietas, heu prisca fides, invictaque bello / dextera!*
  - `l`: "Alas the piety, alas the faith of old, and unconquered in war / right hand!"
  - `i`: "Ah, his goodness, his old-fashioned honour, and that right hand no battle would ever have beaten!"
  - Avoided "Alas for piety, alas for ancient faith", "mirror of ancient faith", "unconquered right hand" in `i`.
- VI.882–883 *Heu, miserande puer, si qua fata aspera rumpas, / tu Marcellus eris.*
  - `l`: "Alas, boy to be pitied, if in any way the harsh fates you could break, / you will be Marcellus."
  - `i`: "Ah, boy we must weep for, if only somehow you could tear the cruel web of fate! You are to be Marcellus."
  - Avoided "child of pity", "child of our mourning", "break through / burst the bonds of fate", "a new Marcellus shall arise in thee", "you shall be Marcellus" (in `i`).
- VI.883–886 *Manibus date lilia plenis… et fungar inani / munere*
  - `l`: "With full hands give lilies, / let me scatter purple flowers, … and let me perform an empty / service"
  - `i`: "Bring lilies by the heaped handful, let me strew bright blossoms; let me at least load my descendant's spirit with these gifts and carry out a rite that can change nothing"
  - Avoided "give me lilies in armfuls / with full hands", "scatter purple flowers" (in `i`), "the empty/vain/useless gift", "though it be in vain".
- VI.893–896 *Sunt geminae Somni portae…*
  - `l`: "There are twin gates of Sleep, of which the one is said / to be of horn, by which to true shades easy exit is given; / the other, wrought of gleaming ivory, shining, / but false dreams to the sky send the Manes."
  - `i`: "Sleep has a pair of gates. One of them, men say, is made of horn, and through it the shadows that speak the truth find a ready way out; the other is finished in white ivory and glitters brightly, but through it the spirits of the dead send up to the world above dreams that deceive."
  - Avoided in `i` "There are twin Gates of Sleep. One, they say, is horn", "two gates the silent house of Sleep adorn", "true shades", "easy passage/exit", "gleaming/glistening ivory", "false dreams", "deluding lies". `l` keeps the literal "twin gates", "true shades", "false dreams" of the Latin word order; reviewer may wish to move "twin gates of Sleep" further from a known version.
